newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian public sector workers take to the streets.
newsitem.headline: Belgian public sector workers take to the streets.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Belgian public sector workers protested noisily but peacefully through Brussels on Wednesday against government plans to reform labour laws and to voice their concerns over pensions and privatisation.
A union spokesman estimated 50,000 workers took part in the march but a police press spokesman put the final figure at 14,400.
The police said there were no reported incidents involving the demonstrators who carried banners and balloons, handed out leaflets and lobbed firecrackers.
"We are here to force the government to wake up to Belgium's problems," a spokesman for the Gendarmerie Federation told Reuters.
"We have come here peacefully now. But next time, if our demands are not met, we will strike nationally," a spokesman for the Liberal Public Service Union, said.

The demonstration was organised by the three main public sector unions, representing some 800,000 staff working in local and national government administrations as well as transport and communications workers.

Among the sectors threatened by full or partial privatisation are state-controlled telephone company Belgacom and postal services. Services already sold off include cross-channel ferry operations and local bus services.
Belgium's military union, Syndic, said it was threatening to call a strike if pay conditions were not improved.
"Since the professionalisation of the military we're suffering financially and 12,000 workers' jobs are threatened," a Syndic spokesman said.
Union leaders accuse the government of breaking promises made after the previous major public sector demonstration in December 1995.
"We want the government to deal with the problems in the public sector instead of hiding behind the Maastricht criteria," a union spokesman told Belgian television.
The government is working on plans to limit wage increases in the public sector to 6.1 percent over the next two years, as well as reform Belgium's pension and social security system.

The government of Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, now in its second term, has been cutting back spending and edging up taxes to bring Belgian debt down in line with the criteria set in the European Union's Maastricht Treaty for participation in Economic and Monetary Union.
Dehaene claims Belgium is well on the way to becoming a founding member of the single currency union due to begin in 1999. European leaders will decide on the 'ins' and 'outs' early next year.
